crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for research data management, first published in 2016, that asks data to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies cover the structured descriptions that make research data findable, and the formal vocabularies that keep those descriptions consistent across systems.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements in which several organisations analyse a combined dataset without any one of them handing over the raw records.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organisation's people, projects, publications, datasets, equipment and their relationships, built so that questions spanning those entities can be answered from one connected source.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation covers the practices and systems that keep digital material readable and usable across decades, well past the life of the hardware and software that created it.

sections.body: Research data and repositories is the part of artificial intelligence work that deals with the material underneath the models: the datasets, the labels, the schemas and the storage systems that make results reproducible and reusable. In practice, AI is being used here to generate metadata at scale, to match records across institutions, to detect duplicates and errors in large collections, and to help build knowledge graphs from scattered documents.The work is less about clever models and more about plumbing, because a dataset that cannot be found, understood or cited is of little use to anyone. Much of it is unglamorous maintenance that determines whether a result can be checked years later.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The principles are settled and widely adopted, and the tooling for describing a dataset with standard metadata is mature enough for routine use. What is not solved is the last mile: metadata is often incomplete or inconsistent, ontologies overlap and conflict, and mapping between them still needs human judgement. Federated sharing of sensitive data works in narrow, well governed settings, but it depends on legal agreements and trusted infrastructure rather than on any technical trick, and it does not remove the underlying privacy risk. Long term preservation is the weakest area, because formats age, storage costs recur and funding for maintenance is rarely secure. Institutional knowledge graphs are promising but frequently stall after the pilot stage, when the effort of keeping them current outlasts the enthusiasm that started them.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a sequence from describing data to keeping it alive. FAIR Data sets out the findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable principles that the rest of the section assumes, and it is the natural starting point. Metadata and Ontologies goes a level deeper into how records are described and how vocabularies are aligned, which is where most practical difficulty lives. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data takes up the case where data cannot simply be copied, covering the governance and technical arrangements that allow analysis across institutions without centralising the records. Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows what happens when those descriptions are linked into a queryable structure across an organisation, and Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the section by asking what survives when projects, formats and funding end. A reader looking for a single overview should start with FAIR Data, and anyone planning infrastructure should read the preservation page before committing to a design.
